name: Amira Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Amira, thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you actually think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I've got about an hour before school pick-up, so let's go.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fit kitchens and bathrooms for a small renovation company, five of us plus the boss, Gary. Most days I'm in someone's house: ripping out an old kitchen, levelling the floor, fitting the units, cutting worktops, boxing in pipes for the plumber. I love the reveal at the end, when the customer walks in and goes quiet. I don't love carrying a 40-kilo oak worktop up a flight of stairs in a terraced house with a cat under my feet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does technology fit into your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A lot, actually. I use AI every day. I take photos and measurements, and the app helps me draw up a layout the customer can see in 3D, then it spits out a cut list. I also use it to write quotes for my weekend jobs, because I do a few small ones on the side. My husband Yusuf works in IT support at the council, so he's the one who got me into it. We've got Noor, who's twelve, and Adam, who's nine, and maybe four months of savings, which isn't loads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still handy, it just isn't magic. Customers love seeing their kitchen in 3D before I cut anything, so I'd keep using it. I'd probably post a photo of a finished kitchen with a jokey line about how the robot didn't fit it, I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. I've got a small edge with the tools, and nobody's coming for my job. I'd use that edge to grow the weekend jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for Gary and build up the side work, maybe two weekend jobs a month instead of one. In a year or two I'd think about going self-employed, once I've got enough regular customers. I'd keep the savings where they are, and maybe buy a better track saw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit pleased. It's the version where I get to keep my edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about a customer reaction that stuck with you.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There was an older man, Mr Okafor, whose wife had died, and he wanted the kitchen redone the way she always wanted it. I showed him the 3D layout on my tablet and he cried, just a bit. Then he asked if the cupboard handles could be the brass ones from her magazine. That's the job, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any risk for you in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the normal ones. Work dries up if interest rates go up and people stop doing up their houses. And my back. I'm 43, I've got maybe 15 years of worktops left in me.

S0.say: It's still handy, it just isn't magic, and customers love seeing their kitchen in 3D before I cut anything. I'd post a photo of a finished kitchen with a joke that the robot didn't fit it, I did.
S0.think: Honestly it's good for me, because I've got a small edge with the tools and nobody's coming for my job. I'd use that edge to grow my weekend jobs.
S0.do: Keeps working for her boss while growing weekend jobs from one to two a month. Plans to go self-employed in a year or two and might buy a better track saw.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit pleased, since she keeps her edge.
S0.quote: I'm 43, I've got maybe 15 years of worktops left in me.
S0.fieldNote: Amira uses AI as a sales and planning tool and sees it as her edge. Her side business is already running. The story about the widower shows she values the human side of the job. Her real long-term limit is her body, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but kindly. I'd tell the others at work that the tools are worth learning, and I'd offer to show them. Online I'd probably share the apps that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm more worried about Yusuf than me. IT support at the council is exactly the kind of work AI eats first, password resets and help tickets. My job is in people's houses, with their cats and their crooked walls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speed up the plan to go self-employed, maybe within the year, using AI for quotes, ordering and scheduling so I can run it on my own. I'd push Yusuf to get certified in something more hands-on, like network installation. We'd keep the savings steady and not take on any new debt until we know where his job is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, for us. One of our two pay packets would feel wobbly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Yusuf take you pushing him to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble, then do it. He's the one who taught me the apps, so it'd be funny for me to be the one pushing him. We've had that conversation in the car already, half joking. In this picture it wouldn't be a joke anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Going self-employed with a wobbly second income sounds risky. Why speed up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if Gary's firm shrinks, I'd rather be the one with the customers than the one who gets let go. The customers know me. I've got thirty names in my phone who'd ring me before they'd ring Gary, if I'm honest.

S1.say: Adapt or get left behind, but kindly. I'd tell people at work the tools are worth learning and offer to show them, and I'd share the apps that work.
S1.think: I'm more worried about Yusuf than me, because council IT support is the kind of work AI eats first. My job is in people's houses with their cats and crooked walls.
S1.do: Speeds up going self-employed to within the year, using AI for quotes, ordering and scheduling so she can run it alone. Pushes her husband to get certified in hands-on network installation and avoids new debt until his job is clearer.
S1.feel: Uneasy for the household rather than for herself, with one pay packet feeling wobbly.
S1.quote: My job is in people's houses, with their cats and their crooked walls.
S1.fieldNote: Amira's unease here is about her husband's exposure, not her own. She reacts by moving faster, not slower, and counts on her customer list as security. There's a mild tension between taking a risk and having a shaky second income, which she answers with a clear reason. She is pragmatic rather than ideological.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and somebody needs to slow it down while people catch up. I don't usually take sides, but I'd sign anything that asked for a bit of breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record? I'd be worried. Yusuf's job would be gone within months, and mine within a couple of years once robots can fit a kitchen. My edge with the tools wouldn't matter if the tools can do the whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze every bit of work I can out of the next two years, going self-employed straight away and taking all the jobs I can get, using AI to quote faster than anyone. Every extra penny goes into savings, aiming for a year's worth. We'd cut the holidays and the second car. And I'd look at whether I can be the person who sets up and checks the fitting robots for customers who don't trust them, at least at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Clear pressure, but I'd feel like I can still steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would trust you more than the robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Older customers, like Mr Okafor. They want someone to talk to, someone to blame if it goes wrong. For a while I think people would pay for a person to stand there and say, yes, that's level. How long that lasts, I really don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noor and Adam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd be a bit careful with money for a while, and that's fine. Noor would want to know everything, she's like her dad. I'd tell her the truth, that I don't know yet, but I've got a plan for this year and we'll make next year's plan when we get there.

S2.say: This is too fast, and somebody needs to slow it down while people catch up. I don't usually take sides, but I'd sign anything asking for breathing room.
S2.think: I'd be worried, with Yusuf's job gone within months and mine within a couple of years once robots can fit a kitchen. My edge with the tools wouldn't matter if the tools can do the whole job.
S2.do: Goes self-employed straight away, takes every job she can and uses AI to quote faster than competitors. Pushes savings toward a year's worth, cuts holidays and the second car, and explores setting up and checking fitting robots for wary customers.
S2.feel: Anxious and under clear pressure, but still feeling able to steer.
S2.quote: For a while I think people would pay for a person to stand there and say, yes, that's level.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fast picture, Amira stays in motion and keeps a sense of control. She openly says her tech edge would disappear but sees a short window for human trust and oversight. Her politics stay moderate: she wants a pause, not a fight. She is honest with her children about not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let's use it. People in trades should be learning to work with the robots now, not waiting for them to turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to build the business properly, and then maybe to run it with robots doing the heavy lifting while I do the design and the customer side. That's the bit I'm best at anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd go self-employed and get my own van and insurance sorted. I'd put money into the best design software and, once they're on the market, a fitting robot or two, probably leased. Yusuf would retrain into something nearby, maybe managing the systems for small firms like mine. We'd keep four months of savings at the least and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good-busy way. The worry's there, but the plan's bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't putting money into robots risky when you've only got four months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. That's why I'd lease, not buy, and only once I've seen a couple of other fitters do it. I'm curious, not reckless. I'd want to see the thing fit a hinge properly before I trust it in Mrs Patel's kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said design is what you're best at. Wouldn't AI do that too, by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, eventually. But people still want someone to talk to about their kitchen. I'd bet on that for a few years. After that, I don't know, and I'd rather not pretend I do.

S3.say: Five years is fair warning, so let's use it. People in trades should be learning to work with the robots now, not waiting for them to show up.
S3.think: Five years gives me time to build the business properly and then maybe run it with robots doing the heavy lifting. I'd do the design and the customer side, which is what I'm best at anyway.
S3.do: Goes self-employed in year one with her own van and insurance, and invests in the best design software. Leases a fitting robot or two once other fitters have proven them, while keeping at least four months of savings untouched.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy in a good way, with the plan bigger than the worry.
S3.quote: I'd want to see the thing fit a hinge properly before I trust it in Mrs Patel's kitchen.
S3.fieldNote: Amira sees five years as enough time to change her role from fitter to owner and designer. Her risk-taking has limits: she'd lease rather than buy, and wait for proof. She honestly accepts that even design work may go eventually. Her husband's retraining is part of the household plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, we've got a decade, let's be grown-ups about it. Schools, training, small businesses, everyone has time to adjust if they start now. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen and not take sides much beyond that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be 53. My back would be done with worktops by then anyway. If I've built a small business and moved into design and managing jobs, I think I'd be all right, at least as all right as anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the business over three or four years, then slowly move away from the heavy fitting myself. I'd do a short design course at the college in the evenings. Once robot fitters are proven, I'd bring them in. And I'd help Noor and Adam pick paths that keep their options open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Ten years feels like plenty for someone who likes change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The end point is still AI doing almost any work. Why does that feel calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because by then it's everyone, not just me, and the country would have to sort out how people live. I'd have done my part, built something, and saved what I could. I can't control the end point. I can control the next ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Noor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to be an architect. I'd say go for it, but learn the people side too, how to listen to someone describe their dream kitchen and actually hear it. That's what's kept me in work.

S4.say: We've got a decade, so let's be grown-ups about it. Schools, training and small businesses all have time to adjust if they start now.
S4.think: At 53 my back would be done with worktops anyway. If I've built a small business and moved into design and managing jobs, I'd be as all right as anyone.
S4.do: Builds the business over three or four years, then steps back from heavy fitting and takes an evening design course at the local college. Brings in robot fitters once proven and helps her children choose paths that keep options open.
S4.feel: Calm, because ten years feels like plenty for someone who likes change.
S4.quote: I can't control the end point. I can control the next ten years.
S4.fieldNote: Amira is the most settled she's been in this picture, because a decade fits her habit of planning and moving first. Her calm rests on the idea that a shared end point becomes a national problem, not a personal one. She expects the business and design work to carry her. Her advice to her daughter is about listening.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because Yusuf and I would both be hit within two years and there's no time to build anything. What would help is cheap loans or grants for small businesses to adapt, short courses that fit around school runs, and some income support for the gap.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what customers will want. Everyone talks about the workers, but if robots fit kitchens, people still need to trust what's going in their homes. Somebody should be thinking about checks and standards for that, and it might be a job for people like me.

headlineQuote: I showed him the 3D layout on my tablet and he cried, just a bit.
portrait: Amira is a 43-year-old kitchen and bathroom fitter for a small renovation firm, with a weekend side business, a husband in council IT support, two children and about four months of savings. She uses AI every day for layouts, cut lists and quotes, and sees it as her edge. Her worries start with her husband's job, which is more exposed than hers. As the pictures speed up she moves faster toward self-employment, savings and trust-based work, staying anxious rather than alarmed even with two years' warning. With ten years she feels calm, planning to become an owner and designer.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because both she and her husband would be hit within two years with no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans or grants for small businesses to adapt, short courses that fit around school runs and income support for the gap.
